final_answer:
No. The trial court did not err (and, on mandamus review, did not abuse its discretion) in disqualifying Smith Fullingham. This scenario tracks In re Zaidi, No. 24-0245 (Tex. Apr. 10, 2026), where the Supreme Court of Texas denied mandamus and left in place an order disqualifying counsel on nearly identical facts.

Rule. Texas disqualification is governed by the disciplinary rules as guidelines, with a high standard of proof; but for side-switching nonlawyer staff (paralegals, legal assistants, secretaries) the Supreme Court has adopted a bright-line framework. In National Medical Enterprises v. Godbey, 924 S.W.2d 123 (Tex. 1996), In re American Home Products Corp., 985 S.W.2d 68 (Tex. 1998), Phoenix Founders, Inc. v. Marshall, 887 S.W.2d 831 (Tex. 1994), and In re Columbia Valley Healthcare System, L.P., 320 S.W.3d 819 (Tex. 2010): (1) a nonlawyer who worked on a matter for one side is conclusively presumed to have obtained confidences, an irrebuttable presumption; (2) a rebuttable presumption arises that the nonlawyer shares confidences with the new firm; (3) the firm can rebut the second presumption only by showing it took minimal prophylactic measures: it must instruct/admonish the nonlawyer not to work on or disclose anything about the matter, and take other reasonable measures to screen her from it (and the nonlawyer must not in fact disclose). If the nonlawyer actually works on the same matter at the new firm, the firm is disqualified as a matter of course (Phoenix Founders; Columbia Valley; American Home Products). The analogous disciplinary rule is Tex. Disciplinary R. Prof'l Conduct 5.03 (supervision of nonlawyer assistants) and 1.09/1.05.

Application. Jones worked on the Apex side of this very suit for about two years, attended strategy meetings and was party to several hundred privileged communications, so the first presumption is conclusively met. Smith Fullingham, Prestige's firm, did no inquiry or admonishment when it hired her in 2017 and let her work on the same Apex-Prestige dispute thirteen times and e-file two documents in 2022; no screening occurred until 2023, after Apex objected. Under Zaidi, the firm must instruct the nonlawyer, at or before the time she begins work on a conflicted matter, not to work on matters she handled for a prior employer, even where the conflict only arises years after hiring, and regardless of whether she was switching sides at hire. The firm failed that, so the second presumption was not rebutted. The firm's responses that Jones does not recall her prior work and disclosed nothing are insufficient: the presumption of sharing is rebuttable only through the prophylactic measures, and her lack of recall, the limited secretarial nature of her tasks, the lapse of time and her time out of the workforce are not substitutes (Zaidi reaffirms the bright-line rule; Phoenix Founders rejected inquiry into actual disclosure). Screening begun in 2023, after she had already worked on the matter, is too late; 'screening going forward' cannot cure prior participation.

Waiver. Disqualification can be waived by unreasonable delay in moving, but waiver is judged from the totality of circumstances and the movant bears no automatic loss from delay; the burden is on the party asserting waiver, and delay must be unexplained and unreasonable and prejudicial (see, e.g., In re EPIC Holdings, 985 S.W.2d 41 (Tex. 1998); In re Users System Services, 22 S.W.3d 331 (Tex. 1999); Vaughan v. Walther, 875 S.W.2d 690 (Tex. 1994)). Zaidi held that e-filing notices listing the legal assistant's name did not establish waiver as a matter of law. Here Apex moved within roughly two months after it actually recognized Jones's name (January 2023 to early March 2023), after seeking an explanation from the firm; this is not an unreasonable delay, and the earlier e-filing notices (March 2022) do not show Apex knew of her employment. Counsel's receipt of notices bearing a name does not equal knowledge of the conflict. The trial court could therefore reject waiver, and Prestige cannot show waiver as a matter of law. Apex also showed no tactical abuse; Prestige's counsel was the party in the best position to screen, and Apex was entitled to rely on her duties.

Assessment. The trial court acted within its discretion; disqualification of the firm was required because the firm did not timely admonish/screen a side-switching legal assistant who actually worked on the same matter. Caveat: I could not retrieve the full text of the Zaidi opinion (court and Justia/CourtListener sites were blocked), so the holdings are verified only through search-result summaries; the precise reporter citation, vote and the details of the waiver standard should be confirmed. Standard of review: abuse of discretion; mandamus review of disqualification orders is available because appeal is inadequate.

issues.text: Whether a side-switching legal assistant who worked on the same matter for the opposing party triggers disqualification of the new firm under Texas law (presumptions, bright-line rule)
Whether the firm's late screening/admonishment (after years of hire and after working on the matter) and her claimed lack of recall rebut the presumption of sharing confidences
Whether Apex waived disqualification by delay, including after e-filing notices bearing her name

claims.text: Texas applies a bright-line rule: nonlawyer's confidences are conclusively presumed, sharing is presumed rebuttably, and the firm is disqualified absent timely admonishment and screening.
Firm's late (2023) screening and Jones's lack of recall do not rebut; firm needed to admonish her at or before she began work on the matter.
Apex did not waive by delay as a matter of law; e-filing notices and a roughly two-month delay after learning of her employment do not establish waiver.
Trial court did not err in disqualifying the firm.
